name: Ute Mountain Homes I
headline: Ute Mountain Homes I will be 15 new rental homes for families earning up to 40% of area median income. The homes are five single-family houses and five duplexes in Towaoc, on the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation. The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe is developing them, and they won a 2026 Round One federal 9% housing tax credit award.
why_it_matters: CHFA calls this the first housing tax credit development in Colorado built on Tribal land and led by a Tribe. The Tribe is the developer, property manager, service provider and sole general partner. The financing is debt-free: the Tribe lends cash-flow-only money and the land comes on a long-term, low-cost lease. That structure can serve as a model for other Tribal nations applying under the Colorado QAP.

status.label: Credits awarded; construction start not confirmed
status.detail: CHFA announced the award on 2026-05-21, and its award report as of 2026-09-30 still lists it. The Tribe's application said it would meet carryover requirements within 13 months of the reservation and place the homes in service within 24 months after the carryover year. There is no public record of a closing, groundbreaking or construction start.

next_step: Watch CHFA's carryover allocation and placed-in-service records, and any public Tribal announcement of a groundbreaking at the East Rodeo Drive site.

key_numbers.meaning: There are 5 two-bedroom and 10 three-bedroom homes in five single-family houses and five duplexes, sized for larger, multi-generational households.
That is about $11.96M over the 10-year credit period, or about $79,761 a year per home (calculated). No state credit is listed.
The application's only two funding sources are tax credit equity and a $1,851,515 cash-flow-only construction-to-permanent loan from the Tribe.
The application commits to a 40-year extended-use period. Four homes are set aside for Special Populations and come with supportive services.

background.text: In its application, the Tribe called this its first LIHTC application and the first and only LIHTC development on the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation. CHFA describes it as the first housing tax credit development in Colorado to be built on Tribal land and led by a Tribe.

The Tribe manages a portfolio of 287 affordable housing units across Colorado, Utah and New Mexico. It has used NAHASDA, the Title VI Loan Guarantee program and the Federal Home Loan Bank's Affordable Housing Program. The application says the Tribe's own resources let it build only a few homes a year, and tax credits let it build 15 at once.
Land deal: the Tribe controls the site through an Agreement to Lease. The application says there is no land cost because of a long-term, low-cost lease, and no property taxes will be assessed.

Financing has no hard debt. The Tribe's cash-flow-only loan means no required debt service, which the application says lets the project serve households at or below 40% AMI. It adds that under NAHASDA, tenants will never pay more than 30% of income on rent.

Demand: the Bowen National Research market study cited a 17.2% simple capture rate. All low-rent units in the market area are fully occupied and managed by the Tribe, and the Tribe keeps a waiting list. The study called the capture rate conservative given overcrowding on the Reservation.

Cost factors named in the application: rural distance (Albuquerque, the nearest major city, is about 275 miles away), a small labor pool, Davis-Bacon wages, and the Tribal Employment Rights Office (TERO) fee of 4% of the construction budget (about $300,000). Shared kitchen and bath layouts and 2- and 4-foot design modules help contain costs.

The application says the Reservation lost its Qualified Census Tract designation in 2026. The Tribe asked for CHFA's discretionary basis boost, saying that without it the federal credit would be $670,352 and the boost would add $276,095 to close a $1,932,665 gap.

Community process: the Tribe discussed the project at a summer 2025 housing retreat and presented it several times to the Tribal Council and its housing advisory board. It also held a public hearing (date not given). The application reports no local opposition.

Residents will have access to services the Tribe provides, including behavioral health, recidivism reduction, vocational rehabilitation, Tiwahe Program service coordination and food distribution. Tribal government offices, a post office and safety services are within two miles.

discrepancies.text: The application requested $946,447 a year in federal 9% credit plus $500,000 in state credit, and its narrative said state credit equity would be a funding source. The award report shows $1,196,414 a year in federal credit and no state credit.
